title: Neuroanatomy, Locus Coeruleus -- Introduction
content: The locus coeruleus is a component of the reticular activating system. See Image. Locus Coeruleus. The reticular activating system comprises the reticular formation, raphe nuclei, and locus coeruleus. It involves many important functions; normally, the reticular activating system mediates consciousness, wakefulness, and attentiveness. The loss of muscle tone during REM sleep is influenced by the caudal third of the locus coeruleus, although the locus coeruleus appears to be mostly inactive during REM sleep in some studies. The locus coeruleus primarily functions through norepinephrine transmission via a g protein-coupled receptor pathway. Arousal, sleep-wake cycle, memory, emotions, and stress are all influenced by the locus coeruleus. [1] [2] [3]

title: Neuroanatomy, Locus Coeruleus -- Structure and Function
content: The locus coeruleus is a nucleus in the lateral floor of the fourth ventricle and upper dorsolateral pons. Norepinephrine, noradrenaline, is a neurotransmitter predominantly released from the locus coeruleus. Norepinephrine helps promote the formation of memories and strengthens memories, especially those created in stressful situations. Noradrenaline released from the locus coeruleus can act on adrenergic receptors (alpha and beta receptors) present on neurons and glial cells (oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, ependymal cells, Schwann cells, microglia, and satellite cells) via adenylyl cyclase and phospholipase C pathways. Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP to cAMP; cAMP then phosphorylates protein kinase A (PKA), which has many functions within the central nervous system. Phospholipase C (PLC) is an enzyme that cleaves phospholipids, resulting in the formation of diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) that contribute to signal transduction pathways. Noradrenaline can also activate glycogen metabolism and calcium signaling in astrocytes, regulating blood flow and blood-brain barrier permeability. [4]

title: Neuroanatomy, Locus Coeruleus -- Embryology
content: Studies on the embryologic development of the locus coeruleus within humans are limited. As the neural tube forms during embryonic development, it divides into segments called rhombomeres in the hindbrain region (see Image. The Hindbrain or Rhombencephalon). In studies performed on mice, researchers discovered that the locus coeruleus originates from the dorsal alar rhombomere 1 (R1). The dorsal subcoeruleus (SubC) also predominantly arises from dorsal alar R1 (Oliveira et al, 2017). Brain development requires regulation via homeobox genes. A homeobox contains a DNA sequence that regulates embryological development and is involved in the segmental organization of the embryo. Engrailed (En) 1 is a homeobox gene that, when expressed, allows the migration of locus coeruleus and SubC to move from ventrocaudal to the basolateral position, placing the structures close to the fourth ventricle.

title: Neuroanatomy, Locus Coeruleus -- Blood Supply and Lymphatics
content: Some studies suggest that activation of the locus coeruleus may lead to increased cerebral blood flow to certain brain areas. Norepinephrine released from the locus coeruleus helps maintain the blood-brain barrier; it leads to vasoconstriction of vessels and may contribute to redistributing blood flow to more active brain areas. The brain receives blood supply from arteries that branch from the circle of Willis. The circle of Willis is comprised of anastomoses of arteries located at the base of the brain. The internal carotid artery and basilar artery are 2 vessels that are part of the circle of Willis. Branches of the internal carotid artery (anterior, middle, and posterior cerebral arteries) supply most of the brain except for the cerebellum, brainstem, and medial occipital lobe, which are supplied by the basilar artery. There has been a long-held belief that the brain does not have lymphatic vasculature. Recently, research has determined that the central nervous system undergoes immune regulation that may take place within the meninges. The discovery of lymphatic vessels or structures within the brain is limited; therefore, further research is necessary.

title: Neuroanatomy, Locus Coeruleus -- Nerves
content: The neurons of the locus coeruleus are mostly branched and not myelinated. Some areas that provide input to the locus coeruleus are the medial prefrontal cortex, hypothalamus, paragigantocellularis, and nucleus prepositus. The locus coeruleus provides output to the hippocampus, spinal cord, hypothalamus, and amygdala. The noradrenergic neurons innervate areas of the brain that help maintain functions such as memory, attention, and the sleep-wake cycle. [5] [6] [7]

title: Neuroanatomy, Locus Coeruleus -- Muscles
content: Rapid eye movement sleep (REM sleep) occurs in about 90-minute intervals and is predominantly a parasympathetic state. REM sleep is also known as paradoxical sleep because beta waves appear on an electroencephalogram. Beta waves are also seen on an electroencephalogram when an individual is awake. Normally, during REM, there is a loss of muscle tone (atonia or tonic muscular inhibition). There is a theory that tonic muscular inhibition is under the control of the caudal part of the locus coeruleus. This decreased muscle tone may protect individuals from inadvertently harming themselves by preventing them from "acting out" their dreams. Lesions of the locus coeruleus and subcoeruleus have been theorized to be 1 possible cause of REM sleep behavior disorder. REM sleep behavior disorder occurs due to the loss of tonic muscular inhibition during REM, leading an individual to "act out" dreams. Depending on the area of the lesion, symptoms can range anywhere from simple limb twitches to complex behaviors such as screaming, laughing, punching, kicking, or running.

title: Neuroanatomy, Locus Coeruleus -- Physiologic Variants
content: Abnormalities of the locus coeruleus have implications as contributing to neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative processes. Individuals suffering from neuropsychiatric processes may be affected due to abnormal norepinephrine regulation, leading to the formation of clinical depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, panic attacks, and anxiety. When norepinephrine becomes elevated, there is an increase in anxiety and mania. Depression may be apparent when norepinephrine decreases. The degeneration of neurons in the locus coeruleus has been postulated as contributing to Parkinson disease and Alzheimer disease. In studies performed on mice, researchers induced the degeneration of locus coeruleus neurons, which resulted in increased deposits of amyloid-beta protein in the brain. Amyloid-beta protein is a component of amyloid plaques. Amyloid plaques are involved in the pathology of Alzheimer disease.

title: Neuroanatomy, Locus Coeruleus -- Surgical Considerations
content: Benefits and risks always merit consideration when contemplating neurosurgery. The locus coeruleus may be damaged during neurosurgery. The tectum of the midbrain is comprised of the inferior and superior colliculi. The superior colliculus functions to process visual information and control eye movement. The inferior colliculus functions to process auditory information. Benign tumors may form in the tectal region of the brain. Neurosurgery for the removal of tumors found in the tectal region is challenging and may contribute to iatrogenic lesions of the locus coeruleus. Damage to the locus coeruleus may result in depression, REM sleep disorder, cognitive difficulties, and more. [8]

title: Neuroanatomy, Locus Coeruleus -- Clinical Significance
content: Locus coeruleus involvement is implicated in processes such as depression, anxiety, Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, and even opiate withdrawal. Medications such as norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, norepinephrine dopamine reuptake inhibitors, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, and alpha-2 agonists act on neurons in the locus coeruleus. Understanding the locus coeruleus can help find the best treatment option for many neurological disorders. Bipolar depression is 1 of many psychiatric illnesses that are difficult to treat. One study observed that when fluoxetine (a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor) was administered independently, the locus coeruleus decreased firing. Administering olanzapine (an atypical antipsychotic) with fluoxetine increased the firing of the locus coeruleus and the levels of norepinephrine release, which helped reduce the overall symptoms of bipolar depression. Increased locus coeruleus activation has implications for the process of opiate withdrawal. Clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist that acts on receptors within the locus coeruleus and decreases the activity of noradrenergic neurons. This decrease in activation of the locus coeruleus can help ameliorate withdrawal symptoms. Other neural mechanisms may be involved in opioid withdrawal; however, more research is necessary. There have been many strides toward the advancement in medicine and understanding of neural mechanisms. Medicine is a continually evolving field, and further research is required to gain an understanding of locus coeruleus involvement in neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. Understanding the structure and function of the locus coeruleus helps determine the best treatment for many neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases that afflict the general population.

title: Neuroanatomy, Locus Coeruleus -- Other Issues
content: MRIs allow non-invasive imaging of the human brain; however, neuroanatomy is quite complex. Many studies to understand pathological processes and the effects of medication are performed using mice or other animals. The mouse brain is similar to that of a human. However, mice may show different physiologic responses in a study. Mice may not experience certain side effects of a medication that a human would and vice versa.
